name: Heaps
tagline: Need the smallest again and again? Keep a heap.
complexity: O(log N) per push or pop, O(N log K) for top K

blocks.html:
An emergency room: the most urgent patient goes next, whenever they arrived. A heap hands you the smallest item in O(1) and stays cheap to update.

Python's heapq keeps it in a plain list.

blocks.text: Example: cheapest way to join ropes

blocks.code:
import heapq

def slow(ropes):                   # brute force: re-sort before every join, O(N^2 log N)
    ropes = list(ropes)
    cost = 0
    while len(ropes) > 1:
        ropes.sort()
        joined = ropes[0] + ropes[1]
        cost += joined
        ropes = ropes[2:] + [joined]
    return cost

def fast(ropes):                   # min-heap: pop two, push one, O(N log N)
    heap = list(ropes)
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    cost = 0
    while len(heap) > 1:
        joined = heapq.heappop(heap) + heapq.heappop(heap)
        cost += joined
        heapq.heappush(heap, joined)
    return cost

for ropes in [[4, 3, 2, 6], [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [7]]:
    print(slow(ropes), fast(ropes))  # -> 29 29, then 33 33, then 0 0
blocks.note: Sort the whole pile every round, then keep a heap

blocks.html: When you keep needing the smallest item from a pile that changes, use a heap. heap[0] is the minimum, and heappush / heappop cost O(log N).

blocks.q: To keep the K largest of N numbers, which heap do you keep?
options: A sorted list of size K
blocks.why: The smallest of your K sits on top, so you can drop it in O(log K) when a bigger one arrives. Total O(N log K).

pitfalls: heapq is a min-heap only. For a max-heap, push -x and negate on the way out.
A heap is not sorted. Only heap[0] is in place; sort the result if order matters.
Tuples with equal first items compare the second. Add a counter as a tiebreak when the second item cannot be compared.
